flawed_step: The proof would need to show that the joint CDF F(x,y)=P(X≤x, Y≤y) can be written using only F_X(x) and F_Y(y). That step can't be justified. The marginals only bound F(x,y) between max(F_X(x)+F_Y(y)−1, 0) and min(F_X(x), F_Y(y)) (the Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds), and the joint CDF can be anywhere in that range.
counterexample: Take two joint distributions on {0,1}^2. (A) Independent fair bits: P(0,0)=P(0,1)=P(1,0)=P(1,1)=1/4. (B) Y=X with X a fair bit: P(0,0)=P(1,1)=1/2, P(0,1)=P(1,0)=0. Marginals check: in A, P(X=0)=1/4+1/4=1/2 and P(Y=0)=1/4+1/4=1/2. In B, P(X=0)=P(0,0)+P(0,1)=1/2 and P(Y=0)=P(0,0)+P(1,0)=1/2. So in both cases X and Y are Bernoulli(1/2). The joint distributions differ, because P(X=0,Y=1) is 1/4 in A and 0 in B.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The marginal distributions don't determine how X and Y depend on each other. Two fair bits that are independent have the same Bernoulli(1/2) marginals as two fair bits with Y=X, but their joint distributions are different. The proof attempt stops at the step that would need to rebuild the joint CDF from the marginal CDFs, which can't be done.
